grounds.point: In or about May 1959, the tenant assigned the tenancy rights to the appellant.
grounds.explanation: The allowed record states that Allen Berry & Co. assigned the tenancy rights to the appellant in or about May 1959. Section 14(1)(b) expressly covers an assignment made on or after 9 June 1952, and section 16(3) separately prohibits a post-commencement transfer or assignment without previous written consent.

grounds.point: The tenant parted with possession of the whole premises to the appellant.
grounds.explanation: The record expressly states that the tenant transferred the lease and put the appellant in possession, and more specifically that it parted with possession of the whole premises. Section 14(1)(b) covers parting with possession, while the supplied report of Parasaram describes the Delhi provision as broad enough to include assignment and other modes of parting with possession.

grounds.point: The transfer occurred after the statutory date specified in section 14(1)(b).
grounds.explanation: The transfer and assignment occurred in 1959. That is after 9 June 1952, satisfying the temporal condition stated in section 14(1)(b).

grounds.point: The supplied record does not resolve whether the lease clause constituted the landlords' written consent to this assignment.
grounds.explanation: The appellant relied on a written lease clause stating that, when necessary to give full legal effect to a covenant or contract, 'THE LESSEE' includes representatives and assigns, and argued that this amounted to written consent. The supplied Delhi provisions require written consent but do not determine whether this definitional clause is sufficient consent to assignment, and the allowed record supplies no resolved finding on that interpretation.

grounds.point: The supplied additional authorities do not eliminate the unresolved written-consent issue for this Delhi assignment.
grounds.explanation: General Radio applies a different Andhra Pradesh rent statute in circumstances where there was expressly no written permission, while its report of Parasaram supports the breadth of Delhi section 14(b) but does not decide whether this target lease clause amounts to consent. Telesound states only a prima facie view in an amalgamation setting and expressly reserves whether the resulting assignment without landlord consent attracts section 14(1)(b), so it supplies no controlling resolution of the target consent question.

grounds.point: The Controller, Tribunal and High Court entered or sustained an eviction order, but the supplied excerpts do not disclose their reasoning on the asserted written consent.
grounds.explanation: The procedural history records an eviction order and unsuccessful appeals. Those results must be preserved at that level, but the allowed scope withholds the target final reasoning and does not establish how the consent clause was treated, so the procedural outcomes cannot fill the decisive interpretive gap.

reason: Assignment, complete parting with possession and the statutory timing requirement are established, but section 14(1)(b) also requires absence of written landlord consent. Because the supplied materials do not determine whether the lease clause relied on by the appellant constituted such consent, the fixed eviction ground remains UNDETERMINED on this record.
